Three steps get you scanning. The rest covers the panel buttons, batch capture and troubleshooting.

The top of the main screen lists four permissions. Tap each button and grant:

• Overlay — lets the panel float above other apps
• Camera — barcode capture
• Accessibility — writes the result into the target app's field (recommended). In system settings it is listed as “Floating scanner injection”: Settings → Accessibility → Downloaded apps, enable that entry
• Shizuku — optional; for systems that only accept key events (e.g. Sixun self-service POS)

A row turns green once it is ready. Scanning still works without the last two, but the text then lands in the clipboard and has to be pasted by hand.
② Start the overlay, put the cursor in place

Tap "Start overlay": a floating ball appears at the screen edge and a persistent notification shows up (the camera is running, Android requires it).

Switch to the app you want to type into — POS screen, notes, Excel — and tap the field to fill.

This is the step people skip: text always goes to whatever has focus. No cursor in a field, nowhere for the keys to land.
③ Open the panel, aim at the barcode

Tap the floating ball to expand the panel and put the barcode inside the preview. The status line walks through "Aim at a barcode" → "Detected: …" → "OK · accessibility (32 ms)".

Once you hear the beep and see OK, move on to the next item.

Ball gestures: tap to expand · drag to move · long-press 600 ms to exit.

• Image — pick a photo and decode the codes in it; no storage permission, works with screenshots and codes received in chat
• Scan page — photograph a whole sheet and type every code on it (next section)
• Test — sends the text from the main screen's self-test field through the full chain; first thing to try when debugging
• Snippets — your saved snippets, tap to send
• Lens — cycles through the available cameras
• Exit — stops the service after a confirmation

The title bar can be dragged; tap Collapse to return to the ball.

A code must be identical across 3 consecutive frames before it is typed, and it is locked out right after until it leaves the frame.

So a label held still under the lens types exactly once. To scan it again, move it out of the frame for at least 1.2 s first.

Two different items in quick succession are both captured: a different code is accepted once 1.2 s have passed.
Whole page: dozens of codes on one sheet

1. On the main screen set Multiple codes in frame to Scan all (whole page). The live preview then stops typing altogether and only frames the shot
2. Open the receiving app, put the cursor in the field, start the overlay
3. Expand the panel and tap Scan page to photograph the sheet

The status line runs Taking photo… → N codes found, typing… → 3/12: xxx → Done: 12/12.

Reading order is top to bottom, left to right within a row; duplicates are typed once; 100 codes per page at most. Gallery photos work too: pick this mode, then tap Image.

Fill the frame with the sheet, keep the phone parallel to the paper and avoid glare. For dense sheets, shoot with the system camera and use Image — it is sharper than the small preview.
Bulk capture into notes or Excel

Leave prefix and suffix empty, turn auto-Enter on, and put the cursor in the body text.

Each scan writes one line and presses Enter, so the cursor moves down by itself. A few dozen serial numbers take minutes, and the result pastes into a spreadsheet one row per line.

Whole-page and gallery batches append to the field; a single scan replaces it — exactly what a POS product field wants.

A profile bundles prefix / suffix / auto-Enter / injection channel / dialog policy. Switch profiles in one tap when you change workstation or target system.\n\nThe profiles screen can export them to a JSON file and import it on another phone, snippets included. Export goes through the system picker: no storage permission, nothing uploaded.
Nothing happens? Check in this order

1. Tap Test on the panel. OK means the channel works and the problem is focus — go back and tap the field
2. The result says blocked by a dialog: the target app popped one and the keys went into it. Use the dialog policy on the main screen
3. The result says copied plus a reason: the original channel failed and the reason follows (Bluetooth not connected, connection timed out, requires Android 9 or newer…)
4. Still nothing: check whether Injection channel is pinned to one option — a profile can lock a single channel
5. Text comes out mangled or full-width: accessibility was unbound by the system. Re-enable it, or use the Shizuku channel

Camera — scans the barcode. Only while the floating window is open; frames are decoded on the device and never uploaded or stored (a page-scan photo is decoded in memory and released right after).

Overlay — keeps the scanner panel on top of the target app (POS, notes, Excel) without stealing input focus. Stealing focus would mean the keystrokes land nowhere.

Accessibility (“Floating scanner injection”) — writes the scanned text into the focused field. It is optional: apps that only listen for hardware key events (old POS terminals) go through Shizuku instead.

Notifications — a foreground notification is what Android requires for a camera service. It is not a push channel.

Bluetooth (Android 12+) — only requested when you use the Bluetooth-keyboard output. Never asked otherwise.

Network — only used by the "Network forwarding" output, and only to the address you type in yourself.

No ads, no analytics SDK, no tracking, no user profiling, no account required.

• Scanned codes, snippets and profiles stay on this phone (SharedPreferences / SQLite) and are deleted with the app.
• Camera frames are decoded on the device by ML Kit. No image or video ever leaves the phone.
• The only network traffic is the address you configure under "Network forwarding"; data goes there and nowhere else, and you can switch it off at any time.
• No device identifiers, location, contacts or any other personal data are collected.
CameraX (preview and still capture), ML Kit Barcode Scanning (on-device decoding), Shizuku (optional shell injection), AndroidX. Each component is used under its own open-source licence.
Full details on network forwarding, the Bluetooth keyboard and the trade-offs behind each design decision are in the project README — see About → Project README.
